newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Trade outlook points to robust U.S. economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Trade outlook points to robust U.S. economy.

text.p: An improving trend for the trade deficit has bolstered expectations that overall U.S. economic growth for the fourth quarter will come in on the strong side.
Several economists also forecast a bright picture for trade going forward, saying the sector could provide added fuel for the economy in 1997.
"Certainly, trade is one of the reasons people are upping their forecasts for fourth quarter gross domestic product," said Kathryn Kobe, economist with the Washington-based firm Joel Popkin and Co.
"The economies of some of our major economic trading partners are beginning to improve. I am expecting net exports to be at least a small positive for the economy in 1997," she said.

Following the release Friday of Commerce Department figures showing the international trade deficit totaled $8.4 billion in November, Kobe bumped up her forecast for fourth-quarter GDP forecast to 3.2 percent from slightly below 3 percent prior to the numbers.

If, as many economists now expect, trade turns out to be a plus for the economy in the final part of 1996, it would be a reversal from the trend for the first three quarters of the year, when the sector was a drag on growth.

Although the gap between exports and imports widened 4.9 percent from the $8.01 billion total recorded for October, the figures for both months represented a sharp improvement from the double-digit monthly deficits seen earlier this year.
The Commerce Department is expected to provide its first, "advance" estimate of fourth-quarter GDP on Jan. 31.
Until a few months ago, many economists had expected expansion in that period to be rather moderate, perhaps only slightly stronger than the 2.1 percent rate of growth posted in the third quarter.
However, several recent economic reports, including data showing robust jobs growth and stronger-than-expected retail sales as well as the trade data, have changed the picture.

"In the last several days, I think we've had to rewrite our view of the U.S. economy in the fourth quarter," said Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich. "The economy in the fourth quarter seemed to have quite a head of steam and is entering 1997 with far more momentum than we thought."

In addition to the trade data, a report from the Federal Reserve on the industrial sector also suggested economic vigor. The Fed said industrial output grew by an unexpectedly strong 0.8 percent in December amid brisk manufacturing activity.
Ehrlich said the trade figures, in particular, will have a "significant positive effect" on gross domestic product growth for the last three months of 1996.
The Commerce official was guardedly optimistic about the trade outlook in 1997.

"I think we ought to be optimistic given the improvements in American competitiveness in the last several years," he said. "American companies have invested in themselves at very high rates. They've adopted new technology and they've tried to reorganize themselves in the face of new technological advances."
One caveat concerning the trade outlook is the risk of weaker-than-expected growth in the major U.S. trading partners that could depress export growth.

Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh, said there are some positive signs for Europe and two key countries, Canada and Mexico. Many economists' predictions for the Japanese economy are less upbeat.
"Of the major trading partners, we're seeing a pickup in growth for everyone but Japan," Berner said.
